intro: Historians of fighting arts rarely watch the past directly. They work from what survives: a painted manuscript in Leeds, a Ming general's handbook, a swordsman's scrolls from Kumamoto, a boxing belt from London, a cup given by a Japanese crown prince, and early films shot in New Jersey and Nevada. Each object was made for its own reasons, and each leaves gaps.

Fighting arts also have a history of refusals. A champion refused Black challengers in the 1880s. Congress refused to let fight films cross state lines in 1912. Muhammad Ali refused the draft in 1967, and the Supreme Court sided with him in 1971. Iceland, Sweden and Norway each closed the ring by law, then later reopened it under licenses.

In this unit you will read objects and legal records as evidence. You will be able to date a source, say what it proves and what it cannot, and explain who held power over a sport at a given moment. You will also compare how the United States, Iceland, Sweden and Norway wrote laws about the ring.
bigQuestion: How do surviving objects and recorded refusals show who shaped the history of fighting arts?

timeline.t: Royal Armouries MS I.33, the oldest surviving European fencing manual, is made
Qi Jiguang writes the Jixiao Xinshu, with a chapter on boxing
Miyamoto Musashi completes the Book of Five Rings near Kumamoto
Muybridge publishes Animal Locomotion, with plates of boxing and wrestling
The Corbett–Fitzsimmons fight is filmed in Carson City, Nevada
Jack Johnson wins the heavyweight title in Sydney
The National Sporting Club awards the first Lonsdale Belt
Congress passes the Sims Act against moving fight films
Muhammad Ali refuses induction in Houston
The Supreme Court decides Clay v. United States
Jack Johnson receives a posthumous presidential pardon

words.d: an object made by people that historians study as evidence
a book written and copied by hand
German for fight book; a late medieval or Renaissance combat manual
a story passed down about the past that cannot be fully proven
a cup, belt or other object given as a prize
an organization that approves contests and recognizes titles
arranged on purpose for a camera or audience
a business person who organizes and sells a match
a racial barrier that kept Black athletes from competing for certain titles
a person who refuses military service for reasons of religion or conscience
an official act that forgives a crime and removes its penalty
laws made by a parliament or congress

test.q: Which object is the oldest known European fencing manual?

test.why: The Ming general Qi Jiguang wrote it around 1560.

test.q: Why do historians separate Musashi's book from stories about him?
choices: Many stories were written long after his life
test.why: Much of Musashi's legend comes from later plays and novels.

test.q: What rule came with the Lonsdale Belt?
choices: It went to the oldest boxer
It was given only to amateurs
Three title wins in one weight class let a champion keep it
test.why: Three title fights won in the same class meant the belt was kept for good.

test.q: What began the sumo Emperor's Cup?
choices: a gift from Crown Prince Hirohito in 1925
test.why: Hirohito's 1925 gift led to the cup.

test.q: What did the wire-mesh mask change in fencing?
choices: It let practice become faster and freer
test.why: With the face protected, fencers could exchange attacks more freely.

test.q: Why were rounds shortened in Edison's 1894 boxing film?
choices: Each round had to fit the film the camera held
test.why: The Kinetoscope held only a short length of film.

test.q: Which state allowed the 1897 Corbett–Fitzsimmons prizefight?
Who refused to fight Peter Jackson?
test.why: Sullivan refused all Black challengers, including Jackson.

test.q: Where did Jack Johnson win the heavyweight title?
test.why: Johnson beat Tommy Burns in Sydney in 1908.

test.q: What did the Sims Act of 1912 forbid?
choices: carrying fight films across state lines
test.why: The Sims Act banned moving prizefight films between states.

test.q: Why did Ali lose his title in 1967?
choices: He refused induction into the Army
test.why: Boxing bodies acted after Ali refused induction.

test.q: What was the vote in Clay v. United States?
test.why: The Court voted 8–0, with Justice Marshall not taking part.

test.q: How did the Nordic boxing bans end?
choices: Licenses and rules replaced outright bans
test.why: Iceland, Sweden and Norway replaced bans with regulated boxing.

test.q: What can a staged photograph of wrestlers not prove?
choices: how a real contest of the time went
test.why: A posed scene may differ from a real match.

write.prompt: Argue from the unit's records: which kind of evidence tells us more about who controlled a fighting art, an object (a manuscript, belt, cup or film) or a legal record (a statute, conviction, court ruling or ban)? Cite two or three by name and date.
tips: Name each source with its date, such as the Sims Act of 1912 or MS I.33 of about 1300.
Say what each source proves and what it leaves out.
Name who held power in each case: a champion, a patron, a court or a parliament.
Label legends as legends and set them beside dated records.
